mcq.q: Which belongs in a metric label?
options: User ID
Prompt text
Model name
Trace ID
mcq.why: Labels must be low-cardinality; IDs and prompts belong in traces or logs.
distractors: One series per user explodes cardinality and cost.
Unbounded values, and possibly personal data.
Unique per request; traces, not metrics, hold it.

mcq.q: Which describes a trace?
options: One request's path: a tree of timed spans sharing a trace ID
A single structured log line written for the request
A numeric time series of request counts per minute
A dashboard panel showing the service's latency
mcq.why: Traces propagate across services, queues and agents.

mcq.q: Metrics are cheap to store and alert on, but lack…
options: Aggregation over time
Per-request detail
Timestamps on each point
Numeric values
mcq.why: Use traces and logs for detail.

mcq.q: How does trace context cross a queue?
options: In message metadata, so async work joins the trace
It crosses automatically with the message body
Through DNS records that name the queue's hosts
It cannot cross a queue, so a new trace starts
mcq.why: The W3C traceparent header covers HTTP; queues need explicit metadata.
distractors: Queues do not carry context by themselves.
DNS does not carry trace context.

mcq.q: What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do?
options: Trains models on the telemetry it collects from services
Receives, processes (sample, redact, enrich) and exports telemetry
Stores dashboards and draws the charts for each team
Replaces the backend store for traces, metrics and logs
mcq.why: It is a pipeline between services and backends.

mcq.q: Why must telemetry export use bounded queues and a drop policy?
options: So a slow backend never blocks requests or fills memory
Because the OTLP protocol requires bounded export queues
To speed up the telemetry backend when it is busy
To deliberately lose telemetry whenever load is high
mcq.why: Count what gets dropped.
distractors: It protects the app, not the backend.
It drops only under pressure, and counts it.

mcq.q: What does a correlation ID do?
options: Links logs, spans, rows and tickets for one task
Encrypts data as it moves across services
Counts the tokens used for billing each tenant
Routes each request to the right replica
mcq.why: The trace ID usually serves this role.

mcq.q: Using user IDs or prompts as metric labels causes…
options: Better, richer dashboards
Exploding cardinality and cost
Nothing worth noting
Faster metric queries
mcq.why: Each unique label value creates a new series.

mcq.q: A team wants its services' telemetry to reach Jaeger today and perhaps a different vendor next year, without code changes. Which protocol should the exporters send?
options: GraphQL
OTLP
CSV over FTP
SMTP
mcq.why: Standard format lets you switch backends.

mcq.q: Which logs are easiest to query?
options: Screenshots of the console
Unstructured stack traces only
Free-text lines in any format
Structured JSON, consistent fields
mcq.why: Consistent fields let you filter and join.

mcq.q: A team labels its request-count metric with user_id. The metrics backend now holds 3 million series and its bill has tripled. What should change?
options: Drop user_id from metric labels; keep it on traces and logs
Sample the metric at 5% to cut the series count
Move the metric to a bigger backend cluster
Hash the user_id so the label values are shorter
mcq.why: Metric labels need low cardinality; per-user detail belongs in traces.
distractors: Sampling metrics loses accuracy and keeps the labels.
That pays for the mistake instead of fixing it.
Hashed values are still one series per user.

mcq.q: A worker that processes upload messages starts a new trace for each message. On-call cannot connect slow ingestion to the upload that caused it. What fixes this?
options: Log the upload's file name in the worker's logs
Use head sampling at 100% for the worker only
Give the worker a longer timeout for each message
Propagate the trace context in the message metadata
mcq.why: Async work joins the original trace when its context travels with the message.
distractors: Names are not reliable links across systems.
Keeping traces does not connect them.

mcq.q: Error rate 1.5% against a 99.9% SLO gives a burn rate of…
mcq.why: 1.5% ÷ 0.1% = 15× (above the 14.4× paging threshold).
distractors: That is the error rate as a multiple of 1%.

mcq.q: What should alerts fire on?
options: User-felt symptoms (SLO burn)
Every log line that is written
Only once a week, in a report
Every CPU spike on any host
mcq.why: Each alert links to a runbook.

mcq.q: At a burn rate of 14.4, how long does a 30-day error budget last?
options: About 1 hour
About 14 days
About 30 days
About 2 days

mcq.q: Error rate 0.5% against a 99.5% SLO. What is the burn rate?
mcq.why: 0.5% / 0.5% = 1, so the budget lasts exactly the window.

mcq.q: Why use multiple burn-rate windows?
options: A slow leak drains the budget without tripping the fast rule
To create more pages for the on-call engineer to handle
To slow alerts down on purpose, so fewer people are woken
Because a single window is not allowed by SRE practice
mcq.why: Fast page, slow page and ticket rules.
distractors: It is allowed; it misses leaks.

mcq.q: Choose all the things a runbook should include.
options: The on-call engineer's password
What the alert means and how to confirm it
Escalation contacts and how to verify recovery
First mitigations: flags, rollbacks, degradation, failover
mcq.why: Runbooks make alerts actionable.

mcq.q: Where should an incident investigation start?
options: From affected traces vs healthy ones, plus recent changes
From the oldest logs in storage, working forwards
From the model's own explanation of what went wrong
From a full restart of every service, to clear state
mcq.why: Check deploys, prompt, model and index versions and provider status.

mcq.q: What makes a postmortem blameless?
options: It skips root causes to save time
It looks at systems, not blame
It has no named author at all
It is never shared with anyone
mcq.why: Action items have owners, including new evaluation cases and alerts.

mcq.q: What should dashboards annotate?
options: Nothing, to keep the panels clean
Every single request that arrives
The team's lunch breaks and meetings
Deploys, model and config changes
mcq.why: Annotations turn charts into investigations.

mcq.q: An alert has no owner and no mitigation. What is it?
options: A runbook entry
Noise, not reliability
A good, useful alert
An SLO for the service
mcq.why: Every alert needs both.

mcq.q: A service has a 99.5% SLO and its current error rate is 2%. What is the burn rate?
mcq.why: The budget rate is 0.5%; 2% ÷ 0.5% = 4.
distractors: That compares the error rate with 1%.
That divides the wrong way round.

mcq.q: At a constant burn rate of 14.4, roughly how long does a 30-day error budget last?
options: About 30 hours
About 7 days
About 2 days
About 14 days
mcq.why: 30 ÷ 14.4 ≈ 2.1 days, which is why that rate pages within an hour.
distractors: That reads the burn rate as days.

mcq.q: HTTP success is 99.98% but grounded answers fell for one language. Which signal caught it?
options: Golden signals on HTTP
AI quality sampling
CPU usage per node
Queue depth and age
mcq.why: Transport health cannot see answer quality.
distractors: HTTP status was fine, so golden signals stayed green.
CPU does not measure answer quality.

mcq.q: Which is an implicit success signal?
options: No rephrase and no ticket afterwards
A thumbs-up given on the answer
A 5-star rating left in the app
A survey answered afterwards
mcq.why: Implicit signals come from behaviour.

mcq.q: Why is “rephrase within 60 seconds” useful?
options: It is a security signal that flags abusive users
It tracks unhelpful answers and is available at once
It measures the cost per request for each tenant
It measures the latency of each answer in seconds
mcq.why: It needs only logs and an embedding similarity check.

mcq.q: Escalations to humans suddenly fall. What could it mean?
options: Quality must be better, so escalations fell
Users stopped using the assistant
Nothing worth investigating
It may have become overconfident
mcq.why: Both too high and suddenly too low are signals.

mcq.q: Answers to HR questions got worse, and retrieval is suspected. Which signals would show a retrieval failure? Choose all that apply.
options: Low top-score queries
Zero-result queries
Abstention rate and citation-validation failures
GPU temperature
mcq.why: Retrieval failures often precede quality complaints.

mcq.q: A model-provider update on day 9 shows up as…
options: More traffic to the assistant overall
Nothing visible on any of the panels
Lower cost per request after the update
More schema failures, less groundedness
mcq.why: The dashboard caught it before users complained.

mcq.q: How should groundedness be monitored in production?
options: By counting the tokens in each answer as a quality proxy
Once, at launch, then never again unless something breaks
Judges on a continuous sample, by feature, tenant, language
Only through user complaints that reach the support team
mcq.why: Sampled evaluation (8.2).

mcq.q: Is the agent saying “complete” a verified task-success label?
options: Yes, if the agent says so
Only for short, simple tasks
No: use outcome events or checks
Only when a judge agrees
mcq.why: Self-reports are not evidence.

mcq.q: Which are agent-specific signals?
options: CPU usage on the hosts that run the agents
Disk I/O on the nodes during each agent run
DNS errors on lookups made by the agent tools
Steps per task, loop triggers, budget exhaustion
mcq.why: They show runaway behaviour.

mcq.q: Which signals belong under safety?
options: Guardrail blocks, injection hits, reports
Latency percentiles for each call
Age of the oldest item in the queue
Token cost per call and per tenant
mcq.why: Track them alongside quality.

mcq.q: A team wants a quality signal it can watch today, without waiting weeks for audit results. Which does the chapter suggest?
options: The agent saying that each task is complete
GPU utilisation on the serving nodes during the day
Monthly customer-satisfaction surveys sent by email
“Rephrase within 60 seconds”, from logs and embedding similarity
mcq.why: It correlates with unhelpful answers and needs only conversation logs.

mcq.q: After an auth change, permission-denied errors on the refund tool jump from 1% to 30%, while HTTP success stays high. Which signal shows this, and where do you look?
options: Golden signals on the gateway; restart the gateway to clear it
Escalation rate to humans; retrain the model on the failures
Per-tool error monitoring by type; check the tool's credentials and scopes
Average latency of the tool; add more replicas to the service
mcq.why: Tool errors are tracked per tool, so a spike points at that tool's permissions.
distractors: The model is not the cause.

mcq.q: Choose all the things an AI trace should let you answer for one request.
options: Which tools ran with what arguments and results
Which prompt version and model were used
The user's home address
What was retrieved (IDs and scores)
mcq.why: Also timings, tokens and cost, and what the user did next.

mcq.q: BM25 and vector search run in parallel. Which is on the critical path?
options: The faster of the two searches
Neither, since they run in parallel
Both, adding their durations together
The slower of the two
mcq.why: Only the slower parallel branch delays the request.
distractors: One of them still sets the time.

mcq.q: Critical path: rewrite 400, max(BM25 40, vector 60), rerank 800, model 850, tool 240, model 2,900 ms, run in sequence. What is the total?
Speeding up a span that is not on the critical path…
options: Always helps the total time
Removes the span from the trace
Changes nothing in total time
Doubles the end-to-end latency
mcq.why: Speed up the longest span on the critical path.

mcq.q: Users say the assistant is slow on Mondays. What did the traces show in the chapter's example?
options: A bigger, slower model was used on Mondays
A slow tokenizer for long weekend messages
Network outages between the two data centres
Rerank waited for a GPU shared with the backfill
mcq.why: That led to separating the reranker pool (15.3).

mcq.q: A worker starts a new unrelated trace. What breaks?
options: The link from its work back to the request
Metrics for the worker's own throughput
The model's outputs for the request
Nothing important for debugging
mcq.why: Propagate context, or link child traces to the parent task.
distractors: The link to the request is lost.

mcq.q: How do multi-agent runs appear in tracing?
options: Child traces linked to the parent
One flat span for the whole run
Separate, unrelated traces
No traces at all
mcq.why: Links keep the run navigable.

mcq.q: Which tools offer LLM-specific trace UIs and accept OpenTelemetry data?
options: k6 or Locust, load testers
Arize Phoenix, Langfuse
Excel or Google Sheets
garak or PyRIT scanners
mcq.why: They show prompts, responses, token costs and evaluations.

mcq.q: A tool times out once after 2 s and then succeeds in 240 ms. How much does the retry add?
options: About 240 ms
Nothing extra
About 4 s
About 2 s
mcq.why: The timeout is spent before the successful retry.
distractors: That is the successful call, not the retry cost.

mcq.q: In the critical-path figure, which change cuts end-to-end time most with the default values?
options: Reducing the tool call by 20 ms
Reducing BM25 (40 ms)
Reducing model call 2 (2,900 ms)
Reducing vector search by 20 ms
mcq.why: The longest span on the critical path offers the biggest saving.
distractors: BM25 is not on the critical path.

mcq.q: What are the four golden signals?
options: Tokens, cost, quality and users
Logs, metrics, traces and alerts
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation
CPU, RAM, disk and network
mcq.why: For AI services, measure them per stage and per model.

mcq.q: Why report latency percentiles rather than the mean?
options: The mean is always higher than the p99 latency
LLM latency is skewed; the mean hides the slow tail
The mean is hard to compute at very large scale
Percentiles are cheaper to store than averages
mcq.why: Report p50, p95 and p99.
distractors: It is lower than the tail.

mcq.q: Which queue signal is the better alert?
options: Queue length right now
Average message size
Age of the oldest item
Number of workers running
mcq.why: Age directly measures delay.

mcq.q: Overnight, schema-validation failures on an extraction endpoint jump from 0.2% to 4%, with no deploy on your side. What is the likely first explanation?
options: A model change
More users
A network outage
A database backup
mcq.why: Track errors by type.

mcq.q: Choose all the saturation signals the chapter lists.
options: Running and waiting sequences
User satisfaction
GPU KV-cache usage
Provider rate-limit headroom
mcq.why: Also connection pools and index node memory.

mcq.q: p50 is flat but p99 climbs from 6 s to 19 s while waiting sequences rise on one replica. What did the chapter find?
options: A provider outage that started that morning
A bug in the tokenizer for long messages
Normal daily behaviour as traffic grows
A tenant's 100k-token prompts filling the KV cache
mcq.why: Per-tenant admission limits and a long-context pool fixed it.

mcq.q: Requests hang instead of failing. What does a low error rate tell you?
options: Traffic must be low at the moment
The model is fast and healthy
Everything is working fine
Little: hangs may not count as errors
mcq.why: Watch latency and queue age too.

mcq.q: Which latencies should be tracked separately for streaming LLM calls?
options: Only time spent in the queue
Only the total time
TTFT, ITL and total time
Only the time to first token
mcq.why: They have different causes (14.2).

mcq.q: In the percentile figure, as the tail gets heavier, what changes most?
options: The median
Nothing
The number of requests
mcq.why: The median barely moves.

mcq.q: Which describes availability as an SLI?
options: Number of replicas running at any time
Average latency across all requests
Uptime of a single server in the fleet
Successful ÷ valid requests, against the SLO
mcq.why: Measured from requests, not machines (15.2).

mcq.q: Of 100 requests, 95 take 1 s and 5 take 21 s. What are the mean and the median?
options: Mean 1 s and median 2.0 s, both fast enough
Mean 2.0 s, median 1 s: the mean matches no real request
Mean 11 s and median 1 s, the mid-point of the two
Mean 2.0 s and median 21 s, set by the slow tail
mcq.why: (95 × 1 + 5 × 21) ÷ 100 = 2.0 s; the median is 1 s, and the slow 5% are hidden by both.
distractors: The median sits among the 95 fast requests.

mcq.q: An ingestion queue's length stays steady at about 500 items, but the oldest item is three hours old. What does this show?
options: Everything is healthy, since the length is steady
Some items are stuck; alert on age, which measures delay
The workers are idle and should be removed
The queue needs a larger maximum size
mcq.why: A steady length can hide items that never get processed.
distractors: Size does not explain the age.

The provider's response, not estimates
Character counts divided by 4

Prompt version
Tenant

None; model tokens are the whole cost

Buy more GPUs to serve the uncached input
Nothing; that mix is normal for any service
Remove the largest tenants from the platform

Nothing in particular for the platform
Training a new model on that tenant's data
Billing, abuse checks, capacity forecasts

mcq.q: GPU utilisation is 95% but cost per successful task is poor. What is the lesson?
options: All is well, since the GPUs are kept busy
Utilisation is not economics; measure cost per success
Buy more GPUs so that requests wait less
Lower the utilisation on purpose to save money
mcq.why: Busy GPUs can still produce failed tasks.

mcq.q: A task makes four model calls and two retries. What should cost reports show?
options: Only the first call's cost for the task
Only the calls that succeeded in the end
The full cost of every call, plus the outcome
Only the last call's cost, with the result
mcq.why: Retries and extra calls are real cost.

mcq.q: Why record the price version with each usage record?
options: For tokenisation of each prompt
For latency measurement per call
Prices change; use the one that applied
For security reviews of the logs

mcq.q: Which self-hosted metric shows real cost efficiency?
options: Model size in billions of parameters
Number of GPUs running per hour
Cost per million tokens served
GPU temperature under load
mcq.why: Include idle hours.

mcq.q: Which token types should a usage record separate?
options: Only total tokens per call
Only output tokens per call
Input, cached input, output, reasoning
Characters and words per call
mcq.why: They have different prices.

options: About $0.0040
About $0.0064
About $0.0036
About $0.0076
distractors: That prices output at the input rate and ignores caching.
That leaves out the cached tokens entirely.
That prices all input at the full rate.

options: The monthly invoice, spread evenly over calls
A different divisor for each language
Word counts multiplied by 1.3
The token counts in each provider response

mcq.q: What is the weakness of head sampling?
options: It is expensive to run on every trace
It keeps every trace that it sees
It decides early, missing rare failures
It needs a GPU to make each decision
mcq.why: Tail sampling decides after the trace completes.

mcq.q: A tail-sampling policy keeps a 5% random baseline of traces. Which other traces should it always keep? Choose all that apply.
options: Every successful fast trace
Slow traces
Low quality scores and flagged safety events
Errors
mcq.why: Plus a random baseline of the rest.

mcq.q: Should metrics be sampled?
options: Only on weekends, at night
No: keep metrics unsampled
Yes, at a 5% sample rate
Only the error metrics
mcq.why: Metrics are cheap aggregates.

mcq.q: Always keep 3% (errors, slow, flagged) plus a 5% random sample of the rest. What share of traces is kept?
What should never be logged?
options: Secrets and auth tokens
Token counts per call
Trace IDs for requests
Model versions in use
mcq.why: Prompts and outputs need per-field decisions; secrets are never logged.

mcq.q: Why alert on dropped-span and queue-full counters?
options: They are required by law for all services
To speed up the exporters under heavy load
A silent pipeline looks healthy and quiet
To reduce the cost of storing the telemetry
mcq.why: Missing telemetry must be visible.

mcq.q: Which is a sensible retention example from the chapter?
options: Full content kept forever, for audits and debugging
Metrics 13 months, traces 30 days, content 7 days restricted
Nothing kept at all, to remove any privacy risk
Everything kept forever in one cheap storage bucket
mcq.why: Audit logs follow legal requirements.

mcq.q: Do deletion requests apply to telemetry?
options: Only to metrics, not traces
No, never to telemetry data
Only to the audit logs
Yes: they reach telemetry too
mcq.why: Traces can contain personal data.

mcq.q: Options for a prompt field in telemetry include…
options: Recorded as a metric label so it can be filtered
Always recorded in full on every span by default
Emailed to the on-call engineer when errors occur
Not recorded, hashed, redacted, or kept in a restricted store
mcq.why: Choose per field.

mcq.q: LLM traces with content can be tens of KB each. What is the main consequence?
options: Nothing changes for the system
Budget storage; strip or sample content
Metrics stop working under load
Traces become faster to search
mcq.why: Telemetry costs are real.

Tail sampling with a higher baseline rate
Longer retention for the stored traces

Retention does not detect missing data.

Sampled evaluation plus input monitoring
Checking CPU usage trends each week

For billing customers by model only
To save tokens on later requests
Aliases change silently; you need to see when

options: Join them to the original trace by ID
Replace all the fast proxy signals
Use them for billing customers only
Ignore them, since they arrive too late
mcq.why: Then report accuracy per prompt and model version.

mcq.q: In the claims-triage example, what did the delayed audit reveal?
options: v14 had 3× v13's overturn rate
The model was perfect throughout
Latency rose sharply after v14
Costs fell sharply after v14
mcq.why: Faster signals had not shown it.

mcq.q: What should you check about proxy signals?
options: That they are cheap to compute
That they track real outcomes
That they are fast to arrive
Nothing; proxies are fine as is
mcq.why: Validate proxies against delayed outcomes.

mcq.q: In the 60-day figure, what caused gradual drift?
options: New product docs never ingested
A prompt change on day 34
The provider model update
The index migration
mcq.why: Gradual drift points to data gaps.

mcq.q: Negative ratings rose after the traffic mix changed. What should you check first?
options: Retrain the model at once on the new questions
Remove the ratings feature from the product
Roll back to the previous provider model
Whether the question mix changed, before blaming the model
mcq.why: Input-distribution monitors separate mix shifts from regressions.

mcq.q: Which freshness signal suits time-sensitive domains?
options: GPU usage per serving node each hour
Answers citing documents past a set age
User login rate per day and per tenant
Token counts per call and per tenant
mcq.why: Plus ingestion lag and index staleness against the SLO.

mcq.q: What should happen on any model change?
options: Re-run the regression suites
Nothing; it is the provider's job
Lower the SLO to absorb it
Delete old traces to start fresh
mcq.why: Changes can break prompts and formats.

mcq.q: An index migration happens on day 12. On the 60-day groundedness chart, what does the line show around that day?
options: Gradual drift
A sharp drop
No visible effect
A sharp rise
mcq.why: Annotations show which events mattered.
distractors: That was the missing product line.

mcq.q: A provider updates the model behind “model-latest”, and groundedness drops on day 30. Traces only record “model-latest”. What should the team change?
options: Lower the groundedness alert threshold so it fires less
Ask the provider to stop updating its models in future
Switch providers after every model update they make
Record the response's model version in every trace, and pin snapshots
mcq.why: Aliases change silently; the response version shows when.

mcq.q: Audits of auto-approved claims arrive 45 days after each decision. A prompt change ships today. Roughly when will the first full week of audited results for it be available?
options: Immediately, because proxy signals stand in for audits
After about 52 days: 45 days of delay plus one week of decisions
After about 45 days, which is the audit delay on its own
After about 7 days, which is one week of decisions
mcq.why: Audits lag by 45 days, and a week of decisions needs another 7.
distractors: Proxies help, but they are not audits.
The week still has to fill.

mcq.q: Why are production failures the most valuable evaluation data?
options: They are synthetic and clean
They are always easy cases
They are real, and they were missed
They are cheap to collect
mcq.why: Make the path from bad trace to test short.

mcq.q: A team wants every production failure to make future releases safer. Which steps belong in its improvement loop? Choose all that apply.
options: Label the root cause and stage
Triage flagged traces
Delete the failing trace
Create an evaluation case and gate releases on it
mcq.why: Then fix the cause, deploy and monitor.

mcq.q: What should be fixed after a failure?
options: Nothing, as it was only one case
Only that exact example, as reported
The test, so that it passes next time
The root cause, not just the one example
mcq.why: e.g. improve parsing for that document type.

mcq.q: What must happen before production text becomes an evaluation case?
options: Publish it as a public example
Nothing; the data is ours to use freely
Redact personal data; get approval if sensitive
Translate it into English for reviewers
mcq.why: Raw customer conversations must not enter shared sets without review.

mcq.q: What does the release gate run?
options: Only the old cases already there
A random sample of the cases
Only the new cases just added
The full suite, old and new cases
mcq.why: See 8.6 and 18.3.

mcq.q: After deploying the fix, what should you check?
options: That the failure signal falls for that category
That traffic rose in the week after the fix
Nothing more; the fix is done once it ships
That costs rose with the release, as expected
mcq.why: Close the loop.

mcq.q: A failing question was fixed and added to the suite as one exact case. A week later a reworded version of it fails in production. Why should paraphrases have been added?
options: For translation into other languages
To confuse the model in testing
To make the suite look longer
So the fix works beyond one wording
mcq.why: One wording can be overfitted.

mcq.q: What tags should an evaluation case from production carry?
options: Links to its trace and issue
The engineer's salary band
The user's full name and email
None at all, to keep it simple
mcq.why: Traceability to the original failure.

mcq.q: Over months, what does the flywheel turn the evaluation suite into?
options: A precise record of users' needs
A marketing document for sales
A training set by default
A random collection of tests
mcq.why: Real failures shape it.

mcq.q: Who should classify a failure's stage (retrieval, generation, tool, data)?
options: The model that failed, explaining itself
The user who reported the bad answer
Reviewers in triage, noting the right behaviour
Nobody; the stage label can be skipped
mcq.why: The stage guides the fix (8.5).

mcq.q: A thumbs-down trace shows wrong answers about scanned invoices. The team adds the exact question with a hard-coded answer to the prompt. What does the chapter recommend instead?
options: Add the question to the training set and skip evaluation
Delete the trace so it no longer appears in the review queue
Fix the root cause, such as parsing, and add the case plus paraphrases
Raise the judge's threshold for that feature
mcq.why: Fixing one example leaves the class of failure.
distractors: The fix must be gated by the suite.

mcq.q: A failing trace includes a customer's name and account number, and the team wants it in the evaluation suite. What must happen first?
options: Translate it into English so all the reviewers can read it
Publish it in the team wiki so others can learn from it
Nothing, since the evaluation suite is only used internally
Redact the personal data, and get approval if the content is sensitive
mcq.why: Production text needs privacy steps before reuse.
distractors: Internal use still needs privacy controls.

mcq.q: What are semantic conventions?
options: A database schema for storing telemetry
Agreed names and meanings for telemetry attributes
A prompt template for model calls
A software licence for OTel libraries
mcq.why: They let tools from different vendors understand your data.

mcq.q: What is the status of the GenAI semantic conventions as of the chapter (checked November 2026)?
options: Withdrawn by the project
Development, not stable
Stable for production
Deprecated for new users
mcq.why: Names and structure can change in breaking ways.

mcq.q: Your dashboards filter on gen_ai.system, and after an instrumentation upgrade the panels go empty. Which attribute superseded it?
options: gen_ai.request.model
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens
gen_ai.provider.name
gen_ai.operation.name
mcq.why: An example of renames under Development status.

mcq.q: Which attributes are opt-in because they are sensitive?
options: gen_ai.usage.output_tokens
gen_ai.request.model
gen_ai.response.id
gen_ai.input/output.messages
mcq.why: Content attributes are off by default.

mcq.q: A team wants to build production dashboards on the draft GenAI conventions. Which steps should it take first? Choose all that apply.
options: Pin instrumentation versions
Assume names never change
Read the status badge per attribute
Map old and new names in the Collector
mcq.why: Also abstract telemetry in one helper and re-check on each upgrade.

mcq.q: Some instrumentation libraries gate the newest behaviour behind which environment variable?
options: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_STABLE
OTEL_GENAI_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL
OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN
OTEL_LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG_GENAI
mcq.why: Check each library's README for supported values.

mcq.q: Where are the GenAI conventions now maintained, per the chapter?
options: Nowhere; the project dropped them
Inside the OTLP protocol specification
A dedicated repo: semantic-conventions-genai
Only on one vendor's website and docs
mcq.why: The old pages point there.

mcq.q: Is OpenTelemetry's maturity a reason to assume the GenAI conventions are stable?
options: Only for its metrics, not traces
Yes, all of OTel is stable now
Only for its traces, not metrics
No: each area has its own status
mcq.why: Check the badge, not the project's reputation.
distractors: Each area has its own status.
Each area has its own status.

mcq.q: Which span name follows the draft convention for a tool call?
options: invoke_tool {tool}
run_tool {tool}
tool_call {tool}
execute_tool {tool}
mcq.why: Others: chat {model}, embeddings {model}, invoke_agent {agent}.

mcq.q: Which metric is in the draft GenAI conventions for token use?
options: gen_ai.client.token.usage
tokens_per_request
llm.usage.tokens.total
openai.usage.total_tokens
mcq.why: Others include gen_ai.client.operation.duration and gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token.

mcq.q: A team's dashboards query gen_ai.* attribute names directly, and the next library upgrade renames several of them. What design makes this cheap?
options: Copying every attribute under both old and new names in code
Freezing the library at its current version for ever
Removing all GenAI attributes from the dashboards
One telemetry helper or Collector mapping layer, with pinned versions
mcq.why: Changing names in one place is cheap; Development status means renames will happen.

mcq.q: Security asks whether the draft conventions record prompts and answers in traces by default. What is the answer?
options: Yes: every span records the full prompt by default
Only token counts, never anything else
No: message content attributes are opt-in and off by default
Only for streaming calls, where it is needed
mcq.why: gen_ai.input.messages and output.messages are sensitive and opt-in.
distractors: Models and finish reasons are recorded too.
Streaming does not change the default.
